# ARC panel marker-count classification

Use when an ARC input has a repeated rectangular grid of panels separated by full-color divider rows/columns, sparse marker cells inside panels, and a smaller output matrix aligned to the panels.

## Procedure
1. Identify full horizontal/vertical divider lines and partition the input into panels, excluding divider cells.
2. For each panel, count cells of the unusual marker color(s), not the separator or base colors.
3. Use all current-instance demo pairs to map each marker count/panel feature to its output value. Verify every output cell; specifically check panels with distinct counts.
4. Apply that mapping to each test panel, with output dimensions equal to the number of panel rows/columns.
5. Validate every output row length and preserve the evidenced fallback value for unobserved counts.

## Solved example and caution
One instance used a 14x7 grid split by divider color 6 into 3x2 panels, each 4x3; the base was 9, marker color 4, and output was 1 exactly for panels with two marker cells, otherwise 9. A distinct demo from the same task used 2x5 panels of size 4x2, base 2, marker 9, with all output values 1; panels contained either one or two markers. Do not blindly equate same task ID with an identical mapping or layout. Demos may vary colors, panel geometry, and observed marker counts. # task-871a8809: extend aligned marker strokes through divided panels

## Confirmed transformation
The grid is partitioned by full divider lines (demonstrated color 8) into a regular matrix of rectangular panels. Sparse colored single-cell markers identify straight, panel-aligned strokes. For each marker color independently:

1. Locate marker-containing panels and their panel coordinates (ignore the precise within-panel marker position).
2. If multiple markers of one color lie in the same panel row, extend a horizontal stroke across all panels between the leftmost and rightmost marker panels, inclusive.
3. If multiple markers of one color lie in the same panel column, extend a vertical stroke across all panels between the topmost and bottommost marker panels, inclusive.
4. Fill each panel along each such stroke completely with that marker color. Keep dividers/background unchanged. When different-color strokes overlap in the same panel, fill the entire overlap panel with color 6 (confirmed for 2/3 intersections).
5. Preserve unmarked panels not traversed by a stroke. Output dimensions equal the input dimensions.

## Evidence
Demo: 22x22, dividers at rows/columns 3, 7, 11, 15, 19; panels are 3x3 (edge panels may be shorter). Color 2 markers are in panel coordinates (0,1) and (4,1), producing a vertical column stroke through panel rows 0–4. Color 3 markers are at (2,0) and (2,4), producing horizontal row stroke through panel columns 0–4. The crossing panel (2,1) is color 6. Strokes fill whole panels, not just marker rows/columns.

Accepted test: 28x28, dividers at rows/columns 4, 9, 14, 19, 24, yielding 6 panel bands per axis. Color 3 endpoints at panel (0,2) and (4,2) gave vertical stroke rows 0–4 in panel column 2. Color 2 endpoints (1,0) and (1,4) gave horizontal row-1 stroke; additional color-2 marker at (3,0) continued a vertical stroke in panel column 0 through rows 1–3. Their overlap at panel (1,2) was 6. Non-traversed panels and divider lines stayed unchanged.

## Validation / cautions
- Recompute separator indices and panel boundaries from each fresh grid; dimensions and edge-panel sizes can vary.
- Work at panel coordinates, then fill every cell in panels along the segments. Do not merely draw a thin line or copy marker cells.
- Separate marker colors before identifying aligned pairs; merge different-color paths only at overlapping panels, using 6 as demonstrated.
- Infer from current demonstrations if a future same-ID variant changes marker pairing or overlap color; this is confirmed evidence, not a guarantee for all variants.",
